clue.text: Good man didn't use the by-pass

definitions.text: Good man didn't use the by-pass

parts.words: Good man didn't use the by-pass
parts.note: in the parable, the priest and the Levite pass by on the other side of the road; the good man of the story is the one who stops to help

explanation.surface: A virtuous fellow avoided the ring road and drove through town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By-pass' suggests a road round a town, but it means passing by: in the parable two travellers passed by the injured man and the third did not.
explanation.definitionFit: The parable's helper from Samaria is the one who stopped rather than passing by the wounded traveller.

clue.text: She confuses the issue

indicators.note: confuses means the letters of the word issue are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman muddles the matter under discussion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confuses' rearranges ISSUE; 'She' is the definition, a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, so it can stand for a she.

clue.text: A fellow gets top prize for a vegetable

parts.note: a fellow is a man
gold is the first prize, the winner's medal

explanation.surface: A man wins first prize at the show for his vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: A mangold, or mangel-wurzel, is a large beet grown mainly for cattle feed.
explanation.definitionFit: A large beet grown as fodder for livestock, a root crop.

clue.text: Rising athletes who lose the final?

definitions.text: Rising athletes who lose the final?

parts.words: Rising athletes who lose the final?
parts.note: runners who go up, or competitors who come second in the last round

explanation.surface: Promising young sportsmen who fall at the final hurdle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising athletes' looks like up-and-coming sportsmen, but read literally it is runners going up; and the losers of a final are second-placed.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who finish second in a contest, losing the last round.

clue.text: No man can keep them waiting, we're told

definitions.text: No man can keep them waiting, we're told

parts.words: No man can keep them waiting, we're told
parts.note: the proverb says these two wait for no man

explanation.surface: Nobody can make them wait, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'time and tide wait for no man' is turned around: no man can keep them waiting.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb holds that the hours and the sea's flow wait for nobody.

clue.text: Fresh market for runners

definitions.meaning: placed before the word market it makes Newmarket, the English racing town famous for horse sales

explanation.surface: A new marketplace for athletes.
explanation.walkthrough: Newmarket in Suffolk is the home of British horse racing and its bloodstock sales; the word before 'market' in its name is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh means recently made; and the word prefixes 'market' to name the racing town where racehorses are sold.

clue.text: Man in the van that's last on the line

definitions.text: Man in the van that's last on the line

parts.words: Man in the van that's last on the line
parts.note: on an old railway train the official rode in his own van at the very rear, the last carriage on the track

explanation.surface: A removal man sits in his van at the end of a queue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Van' suggests a delivery lorry and 'line' a queue, but this is a railway train, whose brake van at the rear carried its official.
explanation.definitionFit: The railway official in charge of a train travelled in the brake van at its tail.

clue.text: Something people want too much to display

definitions.text: Something people want too much to display

parts.words: Something people want too much to display
parts.note: read as a quality shown by those who want too much, rather than a thing too precious to show

explanation.surface: An item people prize too highly to put on show.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a treasure too precious to show; read again, it is the vice displayed by people who want too much.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice is the vice of wanting more than one needs.

clue.text: Put in a word for the opposition

definitions.text: Put in a word for the opposition

parts.words: Put in a word for the opposition
parts.note: not speaking up for rival politicians, but a word expressing the opposite meaning

explanation.surface: Speak up on behalf of the other side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put in a word for' is to recommend; read literally, it is a word that stands for opposition of meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A word of contrary meaning to another, as hot is to cold.

clue.text: First-aid equipment for, military line-ups?

definitions.meaning: a drill term for soldiers aligning themselves in straight ranks

explanation.surface: Medical kit for soldiers on parade.
explanation.walkthrough: Soldiers 'dress' ranks when they align on the man beside them; the stray comma after 'for' is a printing blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: Wound coverings are bandages; and soldiers aligning in ranks is the drill sense of the word.

clue.text: 7 of 7!

parts.note: the cross-reference points to the entry at 7 down, a word of opposite meaning; the opposite of an opposite is a word of the same meaning

explanation.surface: A puzzling numerical riddle, seven of seven.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR read the exclamation mark as a 1. Entry 7 is ANTONYM; the antonym of 'antonym' is a word meaning the same thing as another.
explanation.definitionFit: A word sharing a meaning with another is the opposite kind of word to one with contrary meaning.

clue.text: Do a Nelson-get to grips!

definitions.meaning: a nelson is a grappling hold in which the arm goes under the opponent's armpit and the hand presses on the neck
to grapple or struggle with someone or something

explanation.surface: An exhortation to imitate the admiral and tackle a problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nelson' looks like the admiral, but a full or half nelson is a hold in the grappling sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Applying a nelson hold is a grappling move, and grappling is the sport itself; to tackle a problem is also to grapple with it.

clue.text: Eat off the land

parts.note: read not as living off the countryside but as eating away the ground itself, as water and wind do

explanation.surface: Forage and live on what the countryside provides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live off the land' is the idiom the surface suggests; here the land itself is being worn away.
explanation.definitionFit: Rivers and weather gradually wear away soil and rock, eating at the ground.

clue.text: Edicts can maybe have un- foreseen consequences

indicators.note: maybe says the letters could be arranged otherwise, so these two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Royal decrees can backfire with results nobody expected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' rearranges EDICTS CAN. The hyphen in 'un- foreseen' is the printed line break.
explanation.definitionFit: Mishaps are by nature unplanned events nobody saw coming.

clue.text: It's important in a build-up

parts.note: a build-up read literally as a building going up, where one foundation block matters most

explanation.surface: A key factor in the run-up to something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Build-up' suggests preparation for an event, but literally it is constructing a building, whose key foundation block is laid at an angle of the walls.
explanation.definitionFit: The foundation block at a building's angle, and figuratively anything essential.

clue.text: It takes a lot to elicit it

definitions.text: It takes a lot to elicit it

parts.words: It takes a lot to elicit it
parts.note: a lot is an item up for sale at auction, and each one draws offers from the room

explanation.surface: Something only great effort can draw out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It takes a lot' reads as 'it needs much effort'; but a lot is an auction item, which draws offers.
explanation.definitionFit: An offer of a price at auction is made for each lot put up.

clue.text: There's no limit to what a sick kangaroo, will do

definitions.text: There's no limit to what a sick kangaroo, will do

parts.words: There's no limit to what a sick kangaroo, will do
parts.note: a kangaroo moves by leaping, and an unwell one would leap less

explanation.surface: An ailing marsupial is capable of anything.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words, 'bound less': a sick kangaroo would leap less. The stray comma after 'kangaroo' is a printing blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: Without limits or edges, infinite.

clue.text: Norma's an odd creature, see!

indicators.note: a creature is something created or made up, so these letters are made into something new

parts.note: taken with its S, Norma is

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that Norma is a strange person, look!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creature' rearranges NORMAS AN ODD. A see is a bishop's diocese; SODOR AND MAN is the Anglican diocese of the Isle of Man.
explanation.definitionFit: A see is a bishop's area of authority, and this is the Church of England diocese covering the Isle of Man.

clue.text: Disgusting quality of Augustus's soup

parts.note: Augustus is the boy in the cautionary verse book Struwwelpeter who refused his soup, crying that he would not eat it

explanation.surface: A complaint about how vile some emperor's broth was.
explanation.walkthrough: Augustus suggests a Roman emperor; he is Soup-Kaspar's boy in Struwwelpeter, who wasted away refusing his soup, which he plainly found horrid.
explanation.definitionFit: Horridness or offensiveness is the quality the boy found in his soup.

clue.text: No such gloom in the families of card-players

definitions.text: No such gloom in the families of card-players

parts.words: No such gloom in the families of card-players
parts.note: Happy Families is a children's card game; such families would know no sadness

explanation.surface: Bridge-playing households are a cheerful lot.
explanation.walkthrough: Happy Families is a British children's card game of collecting family sets; families that are happy have none of the opposite feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloom is sadness, the opposite of the happiness the card game's families are named for.

clue.text: Paying attention to the fuel he'd processed

indicators.note: processed says these words are put through a treatment that changes their order

explanation.surface: Being careful about the fuel he refined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Processed' rearranges FUEL HED, the apostrophe dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Being mindful or attentive, taking notice.

clue.text: Empty words-sort' of light

definitions.meaning: idle talk or boasting, hot air
lamps once burned coal-derived fuel in streets and homes

explanation.surface: Idle chatter dismissed as mere lightweight stuff.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle chatter is called hot air in slang; and a lamp burning fuel vapour was a common street light.

clue.text: An old cab — or its disagreeable occupant?

definitions.meaning: a four-wheeled horse-drawn cab of Victorian London, named for the noise it made

explanation.surface: A Victorian cab, or the grumpy passenger inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian four-wheeler was nicknamed for its rumble; and an irritable person snarls like a dog.

clue.text: Man's judges

parts.note: Man is the Isle of Man, whose two senior judges have their own title

explanation.surface: Humanity's arbiters, the judges of mankind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like mankind but is the Isle of Man, a self-governing island in the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The two senior justices of the Isle of Man bear this ancient title.

clue.text: State of a 'street in Paris ?

parts.note: a street in Paris is a rue, and rue also means regret, so the condition of feeling rue

explanation.surface: Asking what condition a Parisian road is in.
explanation.walkthrough: The French for street, rue, is also an English word for regret; feeling rue is the answer's state.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling regret or remorse, a contrite state.

clue.text: Snoring back in clubs ? Quite the contrary

indicators.note: back says the word snoring is read from end to start
in says the clubs are found inside that word
quite the contrary turns the clue around, so it is the clubs in the backwards word rather than the word in the clubs

explanation.surface: A golfer dozing in the clubhouse, or the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: Read SNORING backwards as GNIRONS and the clubs sit inside it; 'Quite the contrary' swaps the clue's 'snoring back in clubs' to 'clubs in snoring back'.
explanation.definitionFit: Golf clubs with metal heads are known by the metal's name.

clue.text: More timid, he goes for the coconut

definitions.meaning: at a coconut shy, a fairground stall, someone throws balls to knock down the coconuts

explanation.surface: A bashful man still has a go at the fairground coconut.
explanation.walkthrough: A coconut shy is a fairground stall where you throw balls at coconuts; one who throws is a shyer.
explanation.definitionFit: More bashful in comparison; and one who throws at a fairground coconut shy.

clue.text: Everybody tries to 'make them

parts.note: tries are attempts, and making attempts is exactly what everybody who tries does

explanation.surface: Something we all attempt to achieve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tries' reads as 'attempts to', but trying is itself making an attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Attempts are what anyone makes when trying something.

clue.text: Took the chair for the early part of the day

definitions.meaning: was seated, or presided over a meeting
the abbreviation for the day Saturday is its first three letters

explanation.surface: Presided over the morning meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The day' is read as the name of a day: the first part of Saturday is its usual abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Being seated or chairing; and the short form of Saturday.

clue.text: Excessively American to go without a covering

indicators.note: to go without means to go outside, so the word for excessively surrounds the letter for American

parts.note: excessively means overly, too much

explanation.surface: An American who goes around without a coat is going too far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go without' sounds like doing without, but here it means going outside, round A.
explanation.definitionFit: A layer laid on top of something, such as a veneer or transparency, is a covering.

clue.text: Go out with a girl

definitions.meaning: to make a sortie, rush out as troops from a besieged place
a girl's name, a pet form of Sarah

explanation.surface: Ask a young woman on a date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go out with' looks like dating; 'with' just links two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A sortie by besieged troops is a sudden rush out; and the word is also a familiar girl's name.

clue.text: In company's he's distinguished as a man of money

definitions.text: In company's he's distinguished as a man of money

parts.words: In company's he's distinguished as a man of money
parts.note: a company officer who looks after the funds; the word for a valued thing is followed by the letter R, as if a precious item, a man of money

explanation.surface: Among a firm's staff, he stands out as the wealthy one.
explanation.walkthrough: In a company or society, the officer who keeps the accounts is the one known as its money man.
explanation.definitionFit: The officer who manages a company's or club's funds and accounts.
